item.title: Incus in One Look: System Containers and VMs in a Single Engine
item.description:
I have two 16 GiB boxes running Debian 13. This series records the whole journey of taking them from bare metal to “two independent clusters plus a self-built console”: concepts, deployment, clustering, storage, networking, migration, ecosystem research, and finally building my own tooling. Part 1 lands the day after Incus 7.0.2 LTS was released (2026-10-29) — an LTS supported until June 2031, a good starting point.

What Incus actually is

One sentence: system containers and virtual machines under the same toolset and the same REST API.

item.title: Storage Choices and Memory Budget on a 16 GiB Box
item.description:
The storage backend decides more than performance — it decides whether migration is a downtime event or a live one. That is the one sentence this post rests on. Along the way: the memory budget for a 16G box, because an uncapped ZFS ARC is a memory thief.

The conclusion first

incus move fundamentally means moving instance disks from A to B:

  • If A and B share one storage (Ceph and friends), no data moves — only runtime state does → live migration, no downtime;
  • With local disks on each node (my case), data is physically copied → downtime migration, seconds to tens of seconds for containers, longer for VMs.

So the first storage question is not “which is fastest” but “am I willing to pay Ceph’s price for zero-downtime migration”. My answer: no. Two 16G boxes cannot carry Ceph’s minimum of 3 monitors + OSDs, and “no mutual replication” makes its replication useless here. Accept the short downtime window on local disks — that is the entire cost.

item.title: Migrated but No Network? The Two-incusbr0 Layer-2 Trap
item.description:
The cluster was up and incus move worked — then came the second big trap of clustering: an instance moves from node1 to node2, its IP changes, the network breaks, and “migration succeeded” turns into “migration incident”. This post explains why, and why I picked OVN out of the three fixes.

Where the trap is: same name ≠ same network

item.title: incus move: What One Command Actually Does
item.description:
This is the heart of the series: “migrate by command” boils down to one line — incus move <instance> --target <member>. But the command’s semantics, boundaries, and common misunderstandings deserve their own post.

One command, four automated steps

bash
1

incus move web01 --target incus-n2

incusd orchestrates four steps after the command: stop, transfer the root disk via zfs send | zfs receive, start on the target node, clean up the source — no manual stop/copy/start needed. The two cards bottom-left mark the key boundary: local storage always means downtime migration (about 5–30 seconds for containers, 1 to several minutes for VMs); shared storage (Ceph) is what enables live migration. Bottom-right: the practical flags and the batch-maintenance entry points.

item.title: One UI for Many Hosts? A Survey of the Incus Web UI Ecosystem
item.description:
The CLI covers the cluster’s needs, but “open a browser and see every machine” never goes away. I went through the Incus-related web UI ecosystem and layered it by “how many hosts can it manage”. Conclusion up front: taking “manage multiple independent clusters” and “one-click cross-cluster migration” together, no maintained open-source project does both.

item.title: One UI for Multiple Clusters: What Open Source Offers
item.description:
The requirement grew: two independent clusters, one per subnet (each starting with a single leader, replicas to follow), one web frontend above both, plus one-click cross-cluster migration. This post separates “intra-cluster migration” from “cross-cluster migration” — they are not the same thing at all — and covers the five hard constraints of going cross-cluster, plus what the open-source survey concluded.

Pinning the topology down

Three layers: a single web frontend at the top (incus-hub / the control plane); below it two clusters sharing nothing — cluster A on subnet 1 (192.168.10.0/24, leader A1 + replica A2) and cluster B on subnet 2 (192.168.20.0/24, leader B1 + replica B2), each internally shaped like the “1 leader + N replicas” from earlier posts. The orange dashed line is cross-cluster migration: copy + delete in essence, with an IP change guaranteed. There is no shared database between the clusters; profiles, networks, and pool definitions are disconnected — that fact creates every difficulty below.

item.title: Building incus-hub: A Console for Multiple Clusters
item.description:
Yesterday’s conclusion was an open-source gap, and of the three roads I picked self-building — evolving the existing incus-hub (a multi-host aggregation page) into a multi-cluster console rather than starting over. This post lays out the design and the order of implementation, and closes the series with the one thing a no-replication architecture owes: backups as the only safety net.

Why evolve incus-hub

Everything v1 has gets reused:

Existing foundation How v2 uses it
Node with zero external dependencies (http/https/fs/path only) Runs directly on Debian 13’s stock Node 20.19.x; the systemd unit already exists
mTLS client certificates + per-host CA Becomes “one certificate per cluster + per-cluster CA”
callNode() / waitOperation() REST helpers Reused for handshake and operation polling
Promise.allSettled partial-failure isolation Upgraded to “a dead cluster greys out, the rest keep working”
Frontend aggregate table + search/filter + demo mode Gains the cluster hierarchy and a migration wizard

Not adapting Orcastra or LXD Mosaic, as covered last post: the former has no public source and wants 4 VMs / 30 GB of control plane; the latter flattens clusters into hosts, is PHP, and last shipped in 2022. None satisfy “light, runnable on Debian 13, controllable”.
